body.p: By the present amendment, the claims have been amended as follows:

Claim 1 has been amended to recite "a camera positioned on a periphery of the multi-functional robotic head, the camera being configured to scan a barcode positioned on a part presented to the robot and capture an image of the part presented to the robot, the barcode providing instructions to the robot for attaching one or more hardware components to the part to assemble the piece of furniture".
Claim 2 has been amended to recite that the "computing unit is further configured to, based on the image captured by the camera, determine dimensions of the part."
Claim 10 has been amended to correct an objection raised by the Examiner.
Claim 16 has been amended to correspond with amended claim 1.
Support for these amendments can be found throughout the application as filed, specifically at paragraphs [0091] and [0094] as well as FIGs. 2-5.

The amendments to the claims have been made without prejudice and without acquiescing to any of the Examiner's objections. Applicant reserves the right to pursue any deleted or withdrawn subject matter in a further divisional, continuation or continuation-in-part application. No new matter has been entered by the present amendment and its entry is respectfully requested/The amendments do not contain new matter and their entry is respectfully requested.

The Office Action dated January 19, 2024 has been carefully considered. It is believed that the amendments submitted herewith and the following comments represent a complete response to the Examiner's rejections and place the present application in condition for allowance. Reconsideration is respectfully requested.
Claim 10 has been objected to because the claim recites "...is one or a slide and a slide spacer."
In response, Applicant has amended claim 10 to recite "...is one of a slide and a slide spacer" as suggested by the Examiner.
Reconsideration is respectfully requested.
The abstract has been objected to because it recites implied phrases such as "Systems, devices and methods for assembling a piece of furniture are described herein."
In response, Applicant has amended the Abstract to remove such implied phrases.
Reconsideration is respectfully requested.

Claims 1-10 and 12 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Chen (U.S. 4,613,942, filed Oct. 22, 1984, hereinafter "Chen") in view or Shinozaki (U.S. 9,649,790, filed Nov. 30, 2012, hereinafter "Shinozaki") further in view of Ross (NPL- IkeaBot: An Autonomous Multi-Robot Coordinated Furniture Assembly System, published May 2013, pgs. 855-862, hereinafter "Ross").
Claims 16, 20-21 and 23-28 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Chen in view of Ross.
Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Claim 1 as amended now recites "a camera positioned on a periphery of the multi-functional robotic head, the camera being configured to scan a barcode positioned on a part presented to the robot and capture an image of the part presented to the robot, the barcode providing instructions to the robot for attaching one or more hardware components to the part to assemble the piece of furniture".

Applicant submits that none of the prior art cited by the Examiner teaches or suggests positioning a camera on a robotic head of a robot for assembling a piece of furniture as claimed in amended claim 1. Applicant submits that positioning the camera 130 on the robotic head 128 as described in the present application provides a number of functional advantages that
are not contemplated in the prior art. For example, positioning the camera 130 on the robotic
head 128 provides for the camera 130 to be movable relative to the part to both scan a barcode
positioned on the part and reliably capture an image of the entire part when the part is on a
conveyor belt.
Chen does not teach or suggest the presence of camera 14 on robot arm 19. Rather, as shown
in FIG. 1, camera 14 is positioned on an opposite side of conveyor 12 from robot arm 19.
As a result of not teach that the camera is movable relative to the part, Chen does not teach
or suggest a camera that is configured to "being configured to scan a barcode positioned on a
part presented to the robot and capture an image of the part presented to the robot" as claimed
in amended claim 1.
Chen specifically does not teach or suggest a camera that is configured to capture an image
of the part to determine dimensions of the part in addition to being able to scan a barcode on
the part. In contrast, Chen only teaches that the camera views the robotic indicia on the part.
The indicia on the printed labels positioned on the parts have four different portions that convey
different forms of information when viewed. Specifically, Chen teaches, beginning at column
2, line 65,
Indicia 13 has a first portion 30 which is formed of a plurality of differently colored dots 31. The color sequence of these dots identifies the part as a specific type of wrench.

A second series of indicia 35 is an equilateral triangle 36, with apex dot 36a which when viewed by camera 14 in conjunction with processor 15 and computer 16 determines the orientation or position of the wrench 11. That is, any rotation about the x-y-z axes, presents a specific triangle image to the camera which is match recognized by processor 15 as a specific angular deviation from the equilateral triangle image as would appear in direct top plan view. This angular deviation is also converted to digital inputs to control the robot arm to the rotation angle to align with the specific angular orientation of the wrench. The third set of indicia 38 is a circle 39 contrasted on background 40. The "size" of the circle, in the camera image, determines the distance of the part from a predetermined fixed or reference point. In addition, with angular deviation from direct top plan view, the circle will appear as an ellipse image to the camera; the size of the ellipse may also provide orientation as well as distance information to the processor. A fourth set of indicia 45 comprises a series of differently colored geometric shapes, e.g., 46, 47, 48, which series identifies the operation which is to be performed by the robot arm with the part. That is, the program for the computer is on the part itself, which program instructs the robot to perform the programmed operation as set forth by the indicia. It is to be noted that the two labels on the part are identical, but placed on different or opposite sides, in case the part is flipped over while
being conveyed.
To summarize the paragraph above, the indicia 13 includes the following:
" a first portion of the indicia that conveys a type of the part;
" a second series of indicia that is used to determine the orientation of the part;
" a third set of indicia to is used to determine a distance of the part from a fixed reference
point; and
" a fourth set of indicia that conveys the operation that is to be performed by the robot
arm 19 on the part.

The second series of indicia and the third set of indicia convey information that is used to determine the orientation of the part and the distance of the part from a fixed reference. The data that is conveyed to the processor, via camera 14, is not necessary to be convey in the present case because of the claimed feature of the camera being positioned on the robotic arm and being able to move to capture an image of the part directly. The image is then used to determine the dimensions of the part.

This is a fundamental difference between the teachings of Chen and claim 1 as amended. In Chen, camera 14 is fixed apart from the robot arm 19 and, therefore, unable to reliably capture an image of the entire part that can be used to determine dimensions of the part.
For the above foregoing reasons, claim 1 as amended is novel and inventive over Chen.

Shinozaki and Ross fail to correct the deficiencies of Chen as each reference also fails to teach or suggest "a camera positioned on a periphery of the multi-functional robotic head, the camera being configured to scan a barcode positioned on a part presented to the robot and capture an image of the part presented to the robot, the barcode providing instructions to the robot for attaching one or more hardware components to the part to assemble the piece of furniture".
Therefore, claim 1 as amended is also novel and inventive over Chen in view of Shinozaki and Ross, either alone or in combination.
Applicant submits that claims 2-10 and 12 are therefore also novel and inventive over Chen in view of Shinozaki and further in view of Ross by way of their dependency on claim 1 as amended.

With respect to claims 16, 20-21 and 23-28, Applicant submits that claim 16 as amended corresponds with claim 1 as amended and therefore is novel and inventive over Chen in view of Shinozaki and Ross, either alone or in combination, for at least the same reasons as provided above in support of claim 1 as amended.
Claims 20-21 and 23-28 are therefore also novel and inventive over Chen in view of Shinozaki and further in view of Ross by way of their dependency on claim 16 as amended.

In view of the foregoing, Applicant respectfully submits that the claims, as amended, are non- obvious, and requests for this rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 to be withdrawn and that the claims, as amended, be allowed.
